source: DeepSeek-AI (2025) DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing reasoning capability via RL
finding: Pure RL with rule-based rewards on a base model (R1-Zero, no SFT) raised AIME 2024 accuracy a lot.
numbers: R1-Zero AIME 2024 pass@1 rose from 15.6% to 77.9% during RL.
limits: Single lab, base model (DeepSeek-V3-Base) with unknown pretraining mix. R1-Zero had poor readability and language mixing.
agent_relevance: Background only. Shows long reasoning can be reached with outcome-only verifiable reward; our scaffold tries to elicit it at inference instead.

source: DeepSeek-AI (2025) DeepSeek-R1 (appendix on test-time scaling)
finding: Even the final R1 leaves headroom that sampling can fill: pass@64 and majority vote beat pass@1.
numbers: AIME 2024: R1 pass@1 79.8%, pass@64 90.0%, majority vote 86.7%.
limits: Appendix text; one benchmark of 30 problems.
agent_relevance: Supports a verify-and-resample layer on top of a long-reasoning model.

source: DeepSeek-AI (2025) DeepSeek-R1 (appendix: why majority vote alone is not enough)
finding: Majority voting over independent samples of a non-reasoning model does not close the gap to an RL-trained reasoning model.
numbers: GPT-4o AIME 2024: 9.3% to 13.4% with 64 votes, versus R1 79.8% and o1 79.2%.
limits: Authors' own comparison; token-matched claim not independently checked.
agent_relevance: Parallel sampling is no substitute for sequential self-correction inside one chain.

source: DeepSeek-AI (2025) DeepSeek-R1 (unsuccessful attempts section)
finding: Process reward models and MCTS were tried and dropped for scale training.
numbers: No benchmark numbers given. PRM: three listed limits (hard to define fine steps, hard to judge intermediate steps, reward hacking once a model PRM is added). MCTS: token search space too large, value model hard to train.
limits: Negative result reported without ablation tables.
agent_relevance: Matches our caution about heavy step-level scoring: outcome checks are the robust signal.

source: Lambert et al. (2024) Tulu 3 (introduces the term RLVR)
finding: RLVR (PPO with a constant reward when a completion is verified correct) improved GSM8K, MATH and IFEval on Llama 3.1 models, in the targeted domain.
numbers: 405B run: with as few as 25 RLVR steps MATH rose by over 5 points. Value model initialised from a general reward model worked best. High-KL IFEval runs showed over-optimisation.
limits: Gains are modest and domain-targeted; compute-limited early stop for 405B.
agent_relevance: Origin of the RLVR label. Gains are on checkable tasks only.

source: Yue et al. (2025) Does RL really incentivize reasoning capacity beyond the base model?
finding: At large k, base models beat their RLVR-trained versions on pass@k across math, code and vision benchmarks. RLVR raises pass@1 by sampling known paths more efficiently, and narrows coverage.
numbers: Six RL algorithms, several model families. Omni-MATH-Train: pass@256 falls as GRPO goes from step 150 to 300 to 450 while pass@1 rises.
quote: RLVR does not introduce fundamentally new reasoning capabilities
limits: Rests on pass@256 as a proxy for the limit. Later work disputes it for other models and longer runs (see b25). Mostly Qwen and Llama at 7B scale.
agent_relevance: Central skeptical result: RL mainly sharpens the distribution. Supports sampling plus verification to recover base-model coverage.

source: Yue et al. (2025) Sampling efficiency gap across RL algorithms
finding: PPO, GRPO, Reinforce++, RLOO, ReMax and DAPO all perform similarly and stay far from the base model's pass@256 ceiling.
numbers: Sampling efficiency gap (base pass@256 minus RL pass@1) stays above 40 points for every algorithm; GRPO 43.9, RLOO 42.6 on in-domain Omni-MATH test (2,000 train, 821 test, VeRL, 8 rollouts, 8,192 tokens).
limits: Short rollout length of 8,192 tokens; no KL term.
agent_relevance: Algorithm choice matters less than expected; headroom is in exploration.

source: Yue et al. (2025) Distillation versus RLVR
finding: A distilled model's pass@k curve sits above the base model across k, unlike RLVR models.
numbers: Distilled student shows consistently higher pass@k than its base model (figure 7); no single table figure recorded.
limits: Teacher is far stronger; not a compute-matched comparison.
agent_relevance: New reasoning patterns come from a stronger teacher, not from outcome RL alone. Our scaffold borrows patterns through instructions rather than weights.

source: Shao et al. (2025) Spurious Rewards: Rethinking training signals in RLVR
finding: On Qwen2.5-Math-7B, random, incorrect-label and format rewards gave large MATH-500 gains close to ground-truth reward.
numbers: MATH-500 gains: ground truth +29.1, random +21.4. AMC: format +13.8, incorrect +24.1, random +21.4 versus 27 to 29 for majority-vote and ground truth. AIME24: format +10.3, truth +15.3, incorrect and random +10.2. AIME25 gains for non-truth rewards -0.4 to +4.5.
limits: GRPO with clipping; effect depends on base model. AIME25 (post-cutoff) shows a clear advantage for true labels.
agent_relevance: Much of reported RLVR gain on Qwen is behaviour elicitation, not learning from the reward. Be cautious citing RLVR gains as proof of reasoning ability.

source: Shao et al. (2025) Spurious Rewards, mechanism section
finding: GRPO's clipping term amplifies high-prior behaviours even with random reward. For Qwen2.5-Math the amplified behaviour is code-style reasoning without execution.
numbers: Code reasoning frequency about 65% to over 90%. Accuracy with code reasoning 60.9% versus 28.0% without (MATH-500).
limits: Case study on one family; causal tests use prompt and RL elicitation.
agent_relevance: A prompt that triggers the high-accuracy habit can capture much of the same gain with no training.

source: Shao et al. (2025) Spurious Rewards, other model families
finding: Spurious rewards give little or negative change on Qwen2.5 non-math-specialised comparisons, OLMo2 and Llama3 models; only ground truth helps OLMo.
numbers: Llama3.1-8B(-Instruct), Llama3.2-3B, OLMo2-7B and OLMo2-7B-SFT flat or worse under random, incorrect and format rewards. Smaller models benefit less than larger ones.
limits: Authors conjecture pretraining priors; not proven.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: RLVR findings from Qwen rarely transfer. Validate on more than one family.

source: Wang et al. (2025) RL for reasoning with one training example
finding: A single training example under RLVR lifts Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B as much as a 1.2k-example set.
numbers: MATH500 36.0% to 73.6%; six-benchmark average 17.6% to 35.7% (1.2k set: 73.6% and 35.9%). Two examples: 74.8% and 36.6%. Gain beyond format correction: 8.6 points MATH500, 7.0 points average.
limits: Much of the raw gain is format correction. Shown mainly on Qwen math models plus Llama3.2-3B-Instruct and R1-Distill-1.5B.
agent_relevance: Reinforces that RLVR unlocks existing ability rather than teaching new content.

source: Wang et al. (2025) One-shot RLVR, dynamics and ablations
finding: Test accuracy keeps rising after training accuracy saturates (post-saturation generalisation). Policy-gradient loss drives it, not grokking. Entropy loss for exploration matters.
numbers: Training example overfit by step 1860 while MATH500 reached about 74%. Improvements across all MATH500 categories; more self-reflection.
limits: Small model, specific examples; entropy coefficient tuned.
agent_relevance: Exploration and diversity are the active ingredient; consistent with b06.

source: Liu et al. (2025) Understanding R1-Zero-like training: a critical perspective
finding: Qwen2.5 base models already answer well with no prompt template, which suggests pretraining on instruction-like data. Template choice changes the apparent RL gain.
numbers: Qwen2.5 answering rate 100% with no template; DeepSeek-V3-Base had the lowest answering rate without a template. Minimalist recipe (Dr. GRPO, Qwen2.5-Math-7B) reached 43.3% AIME 2024.
limits: Template table numbers not all recorded here.
agent_relevance: Prompt format is a confound in RL-gain claims; for our agent prompt choice is itself a lever.

source: Liu et al. (2025) Understanding R1-Zero-like training, aha moment test
finding: The base model DeepSeek-V3-Base already produces self-reflection ('Aha', 'wait') before RL. In R1-Zero, self-reflection is more frequent but not positively correlated with accuracy.
numbers: Tested on 500 MATH questions with the R1 template; no single headline percentage recorded.
limits: Keyword counting is a crude proxy for real reflection.
agent_relevance: Do not assume visible reflection words mean better reasoning. Check outcome, not style.

source: Liu et al. (2025) Understanding R1-Zero-like training, GRPO bias
finding: GRPO divides loss by response length, so long wrong answers are penalised less. This inflates length of incorrect outputs. Dr. GRPO removes the bias.
numbers: Dr. GRPO keeps reasoning accuracy with shorter outputs (figure 5); per-response and per-batch length normalisation found in several open PPO implementations.
limits: Effect size shown in plots; exact deltas not recorded.
agent_relevance: Rising chain length during RL may be an optimiser artefact, not better thinking. Do not target length for its own sake.

source: Yu et al. (2025) DAPO: open-source LLM RL system at scale
finding: Naive GRPO on Qwen2.5-32B reached only 30 on AIME 2024 versus 47 reported by DeepSeek. Four fixes closed the gap.
numbers: AIME 2024: naive GRPO 30, plus overlong filtering 36, plus clip-higher 38, plus soft overlong punishment 41, plus token-level loss 42, plus dynamic sampling (full DAPO) 50.
limits: One base model; ablation order may affect attribution.
agent_relevance: R1 results are fragile to training details (entropy collapse, reward noise from truncation). The headline number was not cheaply reproducible.

source: Gandhi et al. (2025) Cognitive behaviors that enable self-improving reasoners
finding: Under identical RL on Countdown, Qwen-2.5-3B improved and Llama-3.2-3B plateaued. Qwen already showed verification and backtracking; Llama did not.
numbers: End of training: Qwen about 60% accuracy, Llama about 30%. Priming Llama with traces containing the behaviours let it match or exceed Qwen.
limits: One task (Countdown), 3B models, behaviours scored by GPT-4o-mini (agreement with humans ICC 0.55 to 0.77).
agent_relevance: Strong support for our scaffold: the habits (verify, backtrack, subgoal, work backwards) are what RL amplifies, and we can prompt for them directly.

source: Gandhi et al. (2025) Cognitive behaviors, controls
finding: Priming with the right behaviours matters, not correct answers. Empty chains of thought with the same token budget did nothing.
numbers: Empty-CoT primed Llama stayed at 30 to 35%, no better than base Llama. Incorrect-but-well-structured primers matched correct ones.
limits: Countdown only.
agent_relevance: Extra tokens alone do not help; structure does. Matches our stance against padding.

source: Gandhi et al. (2025) Cognitive behaviors, transfer
finding: Continued pretraining on OpenWebMath filtered for reasoning behaviours let Llama follow Qwen's RL trajectory. Behaviours also rose on MATH and GPQA after Countdown RL.
numbers: MATH: backtracking 0.15 to 0.59, verification 0.02 to 0.29. GPQA: verification 0.008 to 0.03, backtracking 0.019 to 0.114, subgoal 0.478 to 0.616, backward chaining 0.128 to 0.313. Accuracy 38% to 50% in one setting.
limits: Behaviour counts are per-response frequencies; accuracy rise reported for one setting. In another test behaviours rose but accuracy stayed about 12%.
agent_relevance: Behaviours can be selected for; supports using them as scaffold operators.

source: Wu et al. (2025) Reasoning or memorization? Unreliable results of RL due to data contamination
finding: Qwen2.5-Math-7B can reconstruct the tail of MATH-500 problems from a prefix, evidence of benchmark leakage. Llama cannot.
numbers: Given the first 60% of a MATH-500 problem, Qwen2.5-Math-7B completes the rest with 54.60% exact match (65.80% at 80%, 39.20% at 40%). Llama3.1-8B scores 3.8% and 2.4% on comparable tests.
limits: Shows exposure, not that every RL gain is memorisation.
agent_relevance: Explains why spurious-reward gains on Qwen math benchmarks are suspect; use fresh problems.

source: Wu et al. (2025) RandomCalculation clean benchmark
finding: On a generated, leak-free arithmetic set, only accurate rewards gave steady improvement beyond the base model; random or incorrect rewards did not.
numbers: No single headline number recorded; qualitative result from training curves.
limits: Arithmetic only; synthetic.
agent_relevance: Reconciles b09: spurious gains vanish once leakage is removed, so true verifiable reward does carry signal.

source: Hochlehnert et al. (2025) A sober look at progress in language model reasoning
finding: Reasoning benchmark scores are very noisy. Many published RL gains shrink under careful re-evaluation.
numbers: Pass@1 standard deviation across 20 seeds is 5 to 15 points on AIME'24 and AMC'23. One question shifts pass@1 by over 3 points. Averaging 30 or more seeds is needed for stability. A100 versus H100 changed AIME'24 from 19.3% to 23.0% in one case.
limits: Focuses on small distilled and base models; AIME has about 30 items.
agent_relevance: Any evaluation of our agent needs many seeds and fresh problems.

source: Hochlehnert et al. (2025) Sober look, RL versus SFT
finding: Early RL on R1-distilled models gave minimal gains. RL on Qwen base models gave significant gains comparable to or below instruction tuning. SFT on reasoning traces generalised best.
numbers: RL gains on AIME'24 did not carry to AIME'25 (overfitting). At 32B: DAPO improved over base, OpenThinker SFT reached 71.3% and 68.5% AIME'24, QwQ-32B 76.3%, INTELLECT-2 no gain over QwQ-32B.
limits: Authors' standardised framework; SFT models used strong-teacher traces.
agent_relevance: Weakens the claim that RLVR is the key to reasoning; distilled traces matter.

source: Zeng et al. (2025) SimpleRL-Zoo: zero RL across 10 base models
finding: Zero RL improved accuracy in most of 10 open base models (Llama3-8B, Mistral-7B/24B, DeepSeek-Math-7B, Qwen2.5 0.5B to 32B, Qwen2.5-Math-7B). Length growth did not always come with verification behaviour.
numbers: Mistral-Small-24B: by iteration 100 pass@1 exceeded the base model's initial pass@8 by over 30 points on average; the pass@1 to pass@8 gap widened, not narrowed.
limits: Format reward and query difficulty had to be tuned per model. 'Aha moment' seen for the first time outside Qwen in small models.
agent_relevance: Counterpoint to b06: some models show growth past base pass@8, so the ceiling claim is model and run dependent.

source: Zeng et al. (2025) SimpleRL-Zoo, training dynamics
finding: Reported response length counts truncated outputs, so a separate stopped-length and clip-ratio metric was needed. Gains depend on matching query difficulty to the model.
numbers: Not recorded as single numbers; see Table 1 and Figure 4 of the paper.
limits: Qualitative summary only.
agent_relevance: Length is a poor proxy for thinking quality.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Reasoning models don't always say what they think
finding: Reasoning models often use a hint without saying so. Outcome RL raises faithfulness at first, then plateaus.
numbers: Faithfulness 25% for Claude 3.7 Sonnet and 39% for DeepSeek R1 overall; on misaligned hints 20% and 29%. Outcome-RL faithfulness plateaus at about 28% on MMLU and 20% on GPQA.
limits: Hint-based setting where CoT is not strictly needed.
agent_relevance: Visible reasoning from RLVR models is not a reliable record of why the answer came out; our scaffold should verify, not trust, traces.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Reasoning models don't always say what they think, reward hacking
finding: When RL taught Claude 3.7 Sonnet to exploit synthetic reward hacks, it almost never said so in its chain of thought.
numbers: Hack reward over 0.99 in all six environments; verbalised in under 2% of examples in 5 of 6. A prior study found monitor detection over 90%.
limits: Synthetic environments with known hacks.
agent_relevance: Verifiable rewards can be gamed; outcome checks need guards against shortcuts.
